# Language structure {#sec-m1-linguagem}

This chapter covers the minimum of the language needed for the rest of the course. The idea is not
to cover R exhaustively, but to recognise the objects we work with and know how to inspect them.

## Objects and assignment

```{r}
tku <- 1250.75          # assignment
uf  <- "PR"
tku
class(tku)
class(uf)
```

Everything in R is an object, and every object has a **class**. When something goes wrong, the first
question is always `class()`. Most of the time, the problem is that a number is
stored as text.

## Vectors

The vector is the basic structure: a sequence of values **of the same type**.

```{r}
ufs  <- c("AM", "PR", "SP", "BA")
tkus <- c(4213386.6, 8332538649.4, 1600854068.7, 1560549752.2)

length(ufs)
tkus[2]                 # indexing starts at 1
tkus[c(1, 3)]
tkus[tkus > 2e9]        # logical indexing: base R's filter
ufs[tkus > 2e9]
```

The types you meet day to day (the names on the left are in Portuguese: numeric, integer,
text, logical, date, factor):

```{r}
c(
  numerico  = class(1.5),
  inteiro   = class(1L),
  texto     = class("PR"),
  logico    = class(TRUE),
  data      = class(as.Date("2026-09-28")),
  fator     = class(factor("Conteinerizada"))
)
```

**Silent coercion** is the main source of errors in real data: if a single value is
text, the whole vector becomes text.

```{r}
#| error: true
x <- c(1, 2, "3")
class(x)
x * 2                   # error: the vector became text
as.numeric(x) * 2       # explicit fix
```

And the missing value, `NA`, propagates:

```{r}
y <- c(10, NA, 30)
mean(y)
mean(y, na.rm = TRUE)
is.na(y)
sum(is.na(y))
```

::: {.callout-note}
`NA` is "I don't know the value"; `NULL` is "does not exist"; `NaN` is the invalid result of a calculation
(`0/0`); and `Inf` is infinity (`1/0`). `is.na()` is the check you will use almost always.
:::

## Factors

A factor is text with a fixed and **ordered** set of categories. It matters because the order
of the levels sets the order of the bars in a chart and of the columns in a table. The
categories below are the ANTAQ cargo profiles: container, dry bulk and liquid bulk.

```{r}
perfil <- factor(
  c("Granel Sólido", "Conteinerizada", "Granel Líquido", "Conteinerizada"),
  levels = c("Conteinerizada", "Granel Sólido", "Granel Líquido")
)
levels(perfil)
table(perfil)
as.integer(perfil)      # the internal code of each level
```

## Matrices

A matrix is a vector with two dimensions. It is the natural structure for an **origin–destination matrix**.

```{r}
od <- matrix(
  c(  0, 120, 340,
     95,   0, 210,
    310, 180,   0),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(origem = c("AM", "PR", "SP"),
                  destino = c("AM", "PR", "SP"))
)
od
dim(od)
od["AM", "SP"]          # flow AM -> SP
rowSums(od)             # total produced by origin
colSums(od)             # total attracted by destination
t(od)                   # transpose
```

In module 3 we will swap `matrix` for **sparse** matrices (`Matrix::sparseMatrix`), which
store only the pairs with flow. That is essential when there are thousands of zones.

## Lists

A list holds elements of different types, including other lists. It is what most
models and routing functions return.

```{r}
cenario <- list(
  nome     = "Cabotagem 2025",
  ano      = 2025L,
  ufs      = c("AM", "PR", "SP"),
  matriz   = od
)
names(cenario)
cenario$ufs
cenario[["matriz"]]["PR", "SP"]
str(cenario, max.level = 1)
```

## `data.frame`

This is the table: a list of columns of the same length. Practically the whole course revolves
around it. From here on, the examples use a real extract of ANTAQ's coastal shipping dataset
that reappears in the rest of the module, instead of made-up numbers.

```{r}
bruto <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx")

fluxos <- data.frame(
  origem  = bruto[["UF de Origem"]],
  destino = bruto[["UF de Destino"]],
  tku     = bruto[["TKU\n(t x km)"]]
)

# a real extract: one row from each of these origin states, plus one
# small shipment, so that the three TKU bands appear in the example
alvo <- c("AM", "PR", "SP", "BA", "SC", "RS")
pequeno <- which(fluxos$tku >= 5e5 & fluxos$tku < 1e6)[1]

fluxos <- fluxos[c(match(alvo, fluxos$origem), pequeno), ]
rownames(fluxos) <- NULL

fluxos
dim(fluxos)
names(fluxos)
str(fluxos)
```

Quick inspection of any table: the four commands you **always** run when you open a
new dataset:

```{r}
head(fluxos, 2)
summary(fluxos)
nrow(fluxos); ncol(fluxos)
sapply(fluxos, class)
```

Accessing columns and rows in base R:

```{r}
fluxos$tku
fluxos[["tku"]]
fluxos[1, ]                       # first row
fluxos[, c("origem", "tku")]      # two columns
fluxos[fluxos$tku > 2e9, ]        # filter
```

## Operators and comparisons

```{r}
2 + 3; 10 / 4; 2^10; 7 %% 3; 7 %/% 3
3 == 3; 3 != 4; 3 < 4
TRUE & FALSE; TRUE | FALSE; !TRUE
"PR" %in% c("PR", "SC", "RS")     # belongs to
```

`%in%` is base R's most useful operator for working with data: it selects everything that is in
a list of codes.

```{r}
sul <- c("PR", "SC", "RS")
fluxos[fluxos$destino %in% sul, ]
```

## Conditionals

The function below classifies a TKU value as high (`"alto"`), medium (`"médio"`) or low
(`"baixo"`).

```{r}
classificar <- function(tku) {
  if (is.na(tku)) {
    "sem informação"
  } else if (tku >= 1e9) {
    "alto"
  } else if (tku >= 1e6) {
    "médio"
  } else {
    "baixo"
  }
}
classificar(fluxos$tku[3])   # SP -> AM, the largest shipment in the extract
classificar(fluxos$tku[7])   # the small shipment we set aside
```

`if` works with **one** value. For vectors, use `ifelse()` or `dplyr::case_when()`:

```{r}
ifelse(fluxos$tku >= 1e9, "alto", "não alto")

dplyr::case_when(
  fluxos$tku >= 1e9 ~ "alto",
  fluxos$tku >= 1e6 ~ "médio",
  .default = "baixo"
)
```

## Functions

Writing functions is what saves you from copying and pasting the same snippet five times. And that is where errors
pile up when you don't.

```{r}
#' Converts TKU to billions of TKU
#' @param tku numeric vector in t x km
#' @param digitos decimal places
tku_bi <- function(tku, digitos = 2) {
  if (!is.numeric(tku)) stop("`tku` precisa ser numérico.")
  round(tku / 1e9, digitos)
}

tku_bi(fluxos$tku)
tku_bi(fluxos$tku, digitos = 3)
```

Things to notice: arguments with a **default value** (`digitos = 2`), input
**validation** (`stop()`) and the fact that the function returns the value of the last expression.

## Iteration

### `for`

```{r}
for (uf in c("AM", "PR", "SP")) {
  total <- sum(fluxos$tku[fluxos$origem == uf])
  cat(uf, ":", tku_bi(total), "bi TKU\n")
}
```

### The `apply` family

```{r}
sapply(fluxos[, "tku", drop = FALSE], mean)      # returns a vector
lapply(c(1e6, 1e9), function(x) sum(fluxos$tku > x))  # returns a list
vapply(fluxos[, "tku", drop = FALSE], mean, numeric(1))  # with a guaranteed type
```

A very common pattern in practice: **read several files and stack them**.

```{r}
#| eval: false
arquivos <- list.files("dados/brutos", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

lista <- lapply(arquivos, readr::read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
base  <- dplyr::bind_rows(lista, .id = "arquivo")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Vectorise before iterating

In R, vectorised operations are faster and more readable than loops. Instead of
going through rows to add two columns, write `df$a + df$b`. Keep `for` for tasks
that depend on a previous step (running a model per scenario, saving files, calling an
API).
:::

## The `|>` *pipe*

The *pipe* passes the result on the left as the first argument of the function on the right. It
turns nested code into a sequence of steps readable from top to bottom.

```{r}
# without pipe
round(mean(fluxos$tku, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9, 2)

# with pipe
fluxos$tku |>
  mean(na.rm = TRUE) |>
  tku_bi()
```

You will also find `magrittr`'s *pipe*, `%>%`, in older material. For what
we will do, the two are equivalent; we will use the native one, `|>`, which needs no package.

## Scripts and algorithms

A script is the recipe: the steps, in order, with comments that say **why** each one
exists. The structure we recommend for any Ministry analysis:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 01-leitura.R
# Goal: read ANTAQ's coastal shipping dataset and standardise columns
# Author: <name>            Last updated: 2026-09-28
# Input:  dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx
# Output: dados/cabotagem_limpa.rds
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. packages ----
library(dplyr)
library(readxl)

# 2. reading ----
bruto <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx")

# 3. standardisation ----
base <- bruto |>
  janitor::clean_names()

# 4. checks ----
stopifnot(nrow(base) > 0, !any(is.na(base$tku_t_x_km)))  # name produced by clean_names()

# 5. writing ----
saveRDS(base, "dados/cabotagem_limpa.rds")
```

`stopifnot()` in the middle of the script is a practice worth the effort: if an assumption stops
holding when the dataset is updated, the script stops where the error is instead of silently producing a
wrong number.
